newsitem.title: USA: Odds seen against Conrail-CSX in merger vote.
newsitem.headline: Odds seen against Conrail-CSX in merger vote.

text.p: A proposed $9.3 billion railroad merger between Conrail Inc. and CSX Corp. faces a crucial Conrail shareholder vote Friday, and some Wall Street analysts said the deal would be defeated in a close vote.
A defeat would create a stalemate between Conrail-CSX and Norfolk Southern Corp., which is pursuing a rival $10.3 billion bid for Conrail, and no clear path to resolving the battle.
Approval would virtually ensure completion of the Conrail-CSX merger, analysts said, although Norfolk Southern is also fighting the deal in court and before federal regulators.
"We think it's obviously going to be a close vote," said Prudential Securities analyst Brian Routledge. "Our guess is that it's leaning toward a 'no' vote."

Both sides were conducting all-out campaigns to woo last-minute votes ahead of the meeting scheduled for Friday in Philadelphia. Shareholders will be voting on whether to exempt Conrail from a state law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail.

A waiver would let CSX complete its $110-a-share cash tender offer to raise its Conrail stake to 40 percent from the current 19.9 percent and give it effective control over Conrail. CSX plans to offer stock for the rest of Conrail, bringing the deal's total value to about $104 a share at Thursday's stock prices.
Norfolk Southern has bid $115 a share in cash for all Conrail shares.
Results of the vote, especially if it is close, were not expected until the weekend or perhaps Monday.
Norfolk Southern has expressed optimism that Conrail shareholders would vote against the deal, while CSX has made cautious expressions of confidence.
"From what we're hearing, we feel very optimistic about prevailing in the shareholders vote on Friday," Norfolk Southern spokesman Bob Fort said on Wednesday.
CSX Chairman John Snow, in an interview on Tuesday, said, "We're reasonably confident, but guarded."
Conrail has said a CSX merger is in the best interests of the company, its employees and other "constituencies," and that Norfolk Southern would be financially depleted if it won.

In addition, Conrail said, the CSX offer is the only realistic one, in view of a two-year "exclusivity period" in the merger agreement between the two firms that prevents both of them from considering a deal with a third party until 1999.

But Norfolk Southern, which has failed to defeat the exclusivity period in court, has sought to woo support by arguing that a vote against the deal on Friday would force Conrail to reconsider Norfolk Southern's higher-valued offer.

The federal Surface Transportation Board last week said it had the power to invalidate the exclusivity period, which it said seemed "excessive on its face," if needed to approve a Norfolk Southern merger with Conrail.
But Conrail said that the board still could not force the railroad to merge with Norfolk Southern against its will.

If shareholders reject the deal Friday, Norfolk Southern has said it would buy 9.9 percent of Conrail -- the most it could without triggering a financially destructuive "poison pill" -- for $115 a share.
Analysts said a defeat could force CSX to raise its offer -- something CSX has said it was unwilling to do -- to attract more support or force all three firms to work out a settlement.
With billions of dollars committed already to the deal, none of the firms can afford to let a stalemate drag out, Prudential's Routledge said.

In addition, the influential shareholder advisory group, Institutional Shareholder Services, said in a report this week that Conrail and CSX would suffer if the stalemate persisted while the railroad industry continues to consolidate.

Analysts and takeover stock specialists said Conrail can count on the 19.9 percent of votes held by CSX and probably another 10 percent to 13 percent held by Conrail employees in stock and benefits programmes.
About 90 percent of the remainder is held by takeover stock specialists and institutions, analysts said.

One takeover specialist said arbitragers would vote unanimously against the deal, leaving institutions with the deciding votes. He said current share prices reflect expectations that shareholders will oppose the merger, and Conrail's stock price would drop if they approve it.
PNC Asset Management Analyst Charles Vincent said votes held by Philadelphia civic and commercial leaders, probably supporting the home-town Conrail, could also be a factor.
"I think its too close to call," he said of the vote.
However, DLJ Securities analyst James Higgins, said in a report this week, "Our sense at this point is that (Conrail) may well lose that vote."
